messages.subject_clean: new line at end of (R)Stan program
messages.body_plain:
On Monday, August 1, 2016 at 4:12:33 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Any idea why there's a problem with new lines in RStan?

The md5sum hash is different with and without the terminating new line, so it thinks that a model on disk (without a new line) is different from the model in memory (where a new line is added automatically).

> We could always pad with a new line.  Could you just
> pad all programs that don't end in newline with a newline
> for doing comparison?

Maybe. I was not sure how to check (in a platform independent way) whether a .stan file on disk ends in a new line or not. When it is read as a string into R's memory, that information is gone.

Ben

Jonah

Just tuning in to also express enthusiasm in this project! (both for improving ADVI/GMO/posterior mode-finders, and validating inference in general)

fyi, there are stochastic unit tests, which operationalize cook, gelman, and robin’s original motivation. That is, rather than produce a deterministic fail/success, a probability of failure is produced, such as the probability that inference is too approximate (or bugged). I don’t suggest we run these tests routinely in every build, but it is nice that we can interpret our fake data checking experiments as actually being unit tests.

Dustin

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev/math] Feature: Torsten (pharmacometrics function library) (#314)
messages.body_plain:
[off issue]

We want to use issues only when the functionality is
well defined enough that unit tests can be written.  We
have wikis and mailing list for general design discussions
before that.

We would also rather have issues broken down into bite-sized
pieces so that they're easy to code review for test coverage.

Software development should not be done by coding and then
adding unit tests and design as an afterthought.  The API,
doc, and unit tests should all be designed together.   A
good API design means something that's easy to test and doc.

The code should be designed top down and implemented
bottom up with unit tests on all the pieces written in tandem
with the code itself.

So it sounds like issue #314 is premature if you don't know
what the unit tests would look like.

- Bob

Btw, I could not create a new branch directly on stan-dev, so I first created a fork -- I don't believe this should pose any problem.
>

messages.body_plain:
This is a directory name gotcha. If there's a `pystan` directory in the
current working directory Python will try to import stuff from there
when you type `import pystan`. You just need to change your directory
(e.g., 'cd /tmp') and things will work. Then it will import pystan from,
as you can see below, `/Library/Python/2.7/site-packages/pystan` where
all the compiled binaries went (including, _api.so, the source of the
import error)

There is a note about this in the documentation.

If you want to have Python install stuff directly into the current
working checkout you can do this: python setup.py build_ext --inplace

messages.subject: refactor coupled_ode_system to use ode_system
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

I intend to refactor the current coupled ode system object. For one reason I would like to align ODE codes (rk45 and bdf) and for two I would like to route execution through the ode_system object. The reason to do so is that we can plug into the system analytic Jacobians of the ODE wrt to states and parameters using partial template specialization's.

To illustrate what I mean, I prepared a "test" which has the sole purpose to show the execution time for the two cases (with AD and without AD):

https://github.com/stan-dev/math/blob/feature/issue-310-coupled_ode_system-refactor-only/test/unit/math/rev/mat/functor/integrate_ode_rk45_noAD_test.cpp

The speed gain for the specific case is close to 2x. This always depends on the ODE system, parameters, etc.. the speed gain will be larger for stiffer systems and for ODE systems with many states (this is my personal guess; the cases with many Jacobian evaluations). Applying this during model inference gave me 2-3x speedups.

Supplying the analytic Jacobians won't be something regular users will, rather only advanced users. Making this user friendly is a different topic (I can share some R codes which help already a lot).

I hold on for the moment with a pull request until the design is settled.

Best,
Sebastian

Charles

messages.body_plain:
Hey,

I read through (much of) your code and examples and I'm trying to understand the difference between the standard Stan ODE solver and your compartmental model functions.  I had a few thoughts:

- Seems like PKModelTwoCpt (and the OneCpt version) are convenience functions in the sense that they wrap up those specific ODE systems for easy use.  They are not really pharma-specific in the sense that other modeling could use them (e.g.-geochemical systems).  Someday it might be nice to have a library of pre-implemented ODE's for a variety of model types like this and starting with pharma-related examples might be a nice thing but for Stan itself it might make more sense to cast them more broadly

- The GeneralCptModel_* functions seem like they are just adapters to use ODE systems with the NONMEM data format---is that right or do they serve another function?

- Then there are a lot of helper functions that make it really slick to use the NONMEM data format (processing multiple events and restarts of the solver associated with the events).  It seems like having
helper functions to turn NONMEM data into a more ODE-compatible format could live separately from the code required to deal with multiple solver restarts associate with events.  That might make it easier for both pieces to get adopted into Stan (and/or the interfaces).

So if I'm mostly correct here, my advice would be to break these things out more if they are going to stand a chance of getting integrated into Stan (even as libraries).  Maybe something like:

1) Some constructs to make it more convenient to use the Stan ODE solvers with multiple restarts (associated with events in your terminology).

2) Some functions to handle converting NONMEM data into whatever more generic format is required by 1)

3) A library of ODE's that implement pharma-specific models and accept data in the NONMEM format.

As is all three seem to be packaged together and that might be hard for the development process to swallow.

Krzysztof

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: [stan-dev/math] Feature: Torsten (pharmacometrics function library) (#314)
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

Great to have this thread! As I have already done projects with Stan in this field of applications, I wrote my own version of Torsten. However, as we "only" have vanilla Stan in our production I used only Stan functionality. I shared a condensed set of this here

https://github.com/stan-dev/example-models/tree/feature/issue-72-stan-pkpdlib/misc/pkpd

I think it needs to be balanced as to what approach we want in going forward. My idea behind the above code is to hide all the boiler plate code for the index fiddling (and ODE restarting) from the user by using the include functionality of rstan. I could have made more use of it. Retrospectively, the constructs which would have made my life easier to program this is

- ragged array structures
- tuples (and ragged arrays of tuples)
- looping constructs over ragged arrays
- a more convenient way to have data variables in my functions (it is a pain to pass from the transformed data block the "x_r" ODE argument through all functions)

Other than that my little library supports analytic and ODE based systems. Features missing in comparison to Torsten are (which I am aware of)

- steady-state conditions (although I have regular dosing); but I am not sure as to how this is implemented in Torsten as it needs an implicit equation solver which we do not have yet in Stan - sundials has such a solver with sensitivity support

- infusions; this can be added, just more index index fiddling and often there are ways to avoid this

I did want to add to the wiki's Charles has started. My apologies for not yet doing so, instead I have written an extensive README which is placed in the branch I point to above.

Best,
Sebastian

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: [stan-dev/math] Feature: Torsten (pharmacometrics function library) (#314)
messages.body_plain:
Hi Krzysztoph,

Thank you for taking the time to read through the code and for the very constructive comments.

I agree with you that Torsten should be broken up, especially since many of its features appear to be extendable to fields other than pharmacometrics. The initial idea was to take a set of functions present in NONMEM and BUGS, and see if we could implement them in Stan. Fitting everything into one function was meant to meet a desired and expected simplicity for the user. I believe one of Torsten's strengths is how accessible and convenient it is for pharmacometricians.

 Evidently, there seems to be a more ambitious and better approach.

> They are not really pharma-specific in the sense that other modeling could use them (e.g.-geochemical systems).

I'm trying to learn about ODE based models in other fields. Right now, my focus in on system biology, but if you have any papers or documents on geochemistry, I am very interested. My hope is to get a better sense of what is pharma specific and what is generalizable in Torsten.

> Someday it might be nice to have a library of pre-implemented ODE's for a variety of model types like this

Agreed. It might even be possible to code the gradients by hand for certain models, and I want to try it out with the one and two compartment models.

> The GeneralCptModel_* functions seem like they are just adapters to use ODE systems with the NONMEM data format---is that right or do they serve another function?

I think you have the right idea.

> It seems like having helper functions to turn NONMEM data into a more ODE-compatible format could live separately from the code required to deal with multiple solver restarts associate with events.

An "internal format", to use Sebastian's term, would indeed be the way to go to make the code more general, and is what has been implemented in Sebastian's code. We should keep in mind that some components of the event schedule could also be parameters. So we would need a wrapper at both ends of the process, one that converts NONEM into the internal format, and one that converts the result back into NONMEM format.

> So if I'm mostly correct here, my advice would be to break these things out more if they are going to stand a chance of getting integrated into Stan (even as libraries).  Maybe something like:
> 1) Some constructs to make it more convenient to use the Stan ODE solvers with multiple restarts (associated with events in your terminology).
> 2) Some functions to handle converting NONMEM data into whatever more generic format is required by 1)
> 3) A library of ODE's that implement pharma-specific models and accept data in the NONMEM format.

This strikes me as a very sensible approach.

(1) would be the "Event Handler" -- currently the pred function in Torsten -- which augments the event schedule and sequentially applies to each event the "solution operator" (to use another very good term Sebastian coins in his ReadMe). It might be a good idea to split pred into two functions that individually handle (i) augmenting the data and (ii) applying the solution operator; mostly because (i) often only involves data and could thus happen in the transformed data block for efficiency purposes.

I would like to find an easy way for the user to specify the solution operator, by letting him:
(a) write the operator in the function block of Stan
(b) write out an ODE system and pick an ODE integrator
(c) call a built-in analytical operator -- currently pred1_one, pred1_two, predSS_one, and predSS_two in Torsten. I am not sure whether these should work with NONMEM data or the internal format in order for them to work with the Event Handler.

Currently, Torsten handles (b) and (c), but it constrains the user to pass in NONMEM data.

> As is all three seem to be packaged together and that might be hard for the development process to swallow.

I would agree with you, though in the end, I think it comes down to only testing 4 functions (currently finishing up unit tests for OneCptModel). Though admittedly, I am not sure on that one.

Andrew, at a recent Columbia - Metrum meeting, suggested using the user mail list to get a better sense of what the community needs in terms of ODE based models, so I'll share the wiki there once it is set up.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: [stan-dev/math] Feature: Torsten (pharmacometrics function library) (#314)
messages.body_plain:
On Friday, August 5, 2016 at 8:46:54 AM UTC-4, Charles Margossian wrote:
> I agree with you that Torsten should be broken up, especially since many of its features appear to be extendable to fields other than pharmacometrics. The initial idea was to take a set of functions present in NONMEM and BUGS, and see if we could implement them in Stan. Fitting everything into one function was meant to meet a desired and expected simplicity for the user. I believe one of Torsten's strengths is how accessible and convenient it is for pharmacometricians.

That's ultimately a great approach to an interface for scientists.  I'm only suggesting making some under-the-hood changes to make that layer thinner and less specialized.

>  Evidently, there seems to be a more ambitious and better approach.

My suggestion is to go for something less ambitious first.  The Stan development process for bringing in small well-specified chunks of functionality is pretty clear and well greased at this point.  At the same time I'm not sure I've ever seen a big ambitious set of changes that went in smoothly.  Maybe Bob/Daniel will just work their magic and see how to integrate all this but

> They are not really pharma-specific in the sense that other modeling could use them (e.g.-geochemical systems).
>
> I'm trying to learn about ODE based models in other fields. Right now, my focus in on system biology, but if you have any papers or documents on geochemistry, I am very interested. My hope is to get a better sense of what is pharma specific and what is generalizable in Torsten.

Bob has some examples in Stan----I can't find them at the moment but maybe he'll pipe up.  I only did some thesis stuff by simulation as an undergrad (it's on floppies somewhere...) so I'm out of touch there.  The other uses I'm familiar with are compartmental models in hydrology and SIR-type compartmental models in infectious disease but again it's not my speciality.

> Someday it might be nice to have a library of pre-implemented ODE's for a variety of model types like this
>
>
> Agreed. It might even be possible to code the gradients by hand for certain models, and I want to try it out with the one and two compartment models.
>
> The GeneralCptModel_* functions seem like they are just adapters to use ODE systems with the NONMEM data format---is that right or do they serve another function?
>
>
> I think you have the right idea.
>
> It seems like having helper functions to turn NONMEM data into a more ODE-compatible format could live separately from the code required to deal with multiple solver restarts associate with events.
>
>
> An "internal format", to use Sebastian's term, would indeed be the way to go to make the code more general, and is what has been implemented in Sebastian's code. We should keep in mind that some components of the event schedule could also be parameters. So we would need a wrapper at both ends of the process, one that converts NONEM into the internal format, and one that converts the result back into NONMEM format.
>
> So if I'm mostly correct here, my advice would be to break these things out more if they are going to stand a chance of getting integrated into Stan (even as libraries).  Maybe something like:
> 1) Some constructs to make it more convenient to use the Stan ODE solvers with multiple restarts (associated with events in your terminology).
> 2) Some functions to handle converting NONMEM data into whatever more generic format is required by 1)
> 3) A library of ODE's that implement pharma-specific models and accept data in the NONMEM format.
>
>
> This strikes me as a very sensible approach.
>
>
> (1) would be the "Event Handler" -- currently the pred function in Torsten -- which augments the event schedule and sequentially applies to each event the "solution operator" (to use another very good term Sebastian coins in his ReadMe). It might be a good idea to split pred into two functions that individually handle (i) augmenting the data and (ii) applying the solution operator; mostly because (i) often only involves data and could thus happen in the transformed data block for efficiency purposes.
>
>
> I would like to find an easy way for the user to specify the solution operator, by letting him:
> (a) write the operator in the function block of Stan
> (b) write out an ODE system and pick an ODE integrator
> (c) call a built-in analytical operator -- currently pred1_one, pred1_two, predSS_one, and predSS_two in Torsten. I am not sure whether these should work with NONMEM data or the internal format in order for them to work with the Event Handler.
>
>
> Currently, Torsten handles (b) and (c), but it constrains the user to pass in NONMEM data.

All of this makes sense and I'm looking forward to the meeting next week.  I'll give Sebastien's code a better read as well.

>
> As is all three seem to be packaged together and that might be hard for the development process to swallow.
>
>
> I would agree with you, though in the end, I think it comes down to only testing 4 functions (currently finishing up unit tests for OneCptModel). Though admittedly, I am not sure on that one.

So far Stan is tested all the way down to the math library so I'm pretty sure we'll need tests for all the pieces here.

Krzysztof

>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] refactor coupled_ode_system to use ode_system
messages.body_plain:
Hi Sebastian,

I think I see what's going on. Let me try to get everyone on board.

These are the three relevant files to look at:
oral_2cmt.hpp <https://github.com/stan-dev/math/blob/feature/issue-310-coupled_ode_system-refactor-only/test/unit/math/rev/mat/functor/oral_2cmt.hpp>
The functor defined here is very close to what would be translated from Stan to C++.
ode_system.hpp <https://github.com/stan-dev/math/blob/300a769011fb7a53aeff495deee6e155280a5ee1/stan/math/rev/mat/functor/ode_system.hpp>
The first functor is passed into this class, ode_system, to calculate Jacobians. Jacobians are required by CVODES. ode_system takes the functor and uses automatic differentiation to compute Jacobians.
oral_2cmt_jacobian.hpp <https://github.com/stan-dev/math/blob/feature/issue-310-coupled_ode_system-refactor-only/test/unit/math/rev/mat/functor/oral_2cmt_jacobian.hpp>
This is a template specialization of the second file, ode_system, but for the oral_2cmt functor. Here, the Jacobians are known analytically so they're computed using doubles and without automatic differentiation.
This is a specialization for just that particular functor and is written in C++. This is currently not generated from the Stan language. In order to write analytic Jacobians in this way, a user needs to perform surgery on the generated code, but it can be done.
Some comments in no particular order:
I'm really pleased that autodiff is only 2x as long as putting in analytic gradients! That's awesome! I know this is a simpler example, but still... that's really rad.
I think there are changes we can make to ode_system to make things a lot better:
Rename. It's not an ode system. It's the Jacobians of an ode system. There are three functions exposed:
1. A function to calculate the value of the ode at the time and state provided.
2. A function to calculate the Jacobian of the RHS with respect to y.
3. A function to calculate the Jacobians of the RHS with respect to y and the RHS with respect to theta.
Clean up the interface. I don't think it needs to be this complicated. For example, here are the three function signatures I would provide:
std::vector<double> operator()(double t, const std::vector<double>& y). returns dy_dt.
For the two Jacobian functions, I would simplify a lot and just use Eigen::Matrix<double, Dynamic, Dynamic> (or whatever the right type is). Having the indirection of Eigen::MatrixBase<Derived1> where Derived1 is a template parameter isn't helping. These things are double based containers and it would help a lot if it weren't overengineered. Unless there's a use-case that I'm missing. It doesn't look like there is, though.
I'd rethink cvodes_ode_data.hpp. I don't understand the naming. Now that I look at it, why aren't the functions in the existing ode_system.hpp renamed to rhs_sens() and dense_jacobian()? Would that be more descriptive?
What are your use cases for having people specify analytic Jacobians? (I guess CVODES is calling them sensitivities and dense Jacobians.)
If the goal is to have a user be able to hack the C++, I think it's sufficient to rename and clean up ode_system. And possibly cvodes_ode_data as well.
If the goal is to have people write sensitivities and dense Jacobians in the Stan language, then what do you expect it to generate? Right now, we don't even allow users to specify gradients on their own functions and I think this is a good thing. Experts will be able to get into the C++ directly. I think it's hard to implement gradients correctly and not allowing users to try has saved us a lot of effort.

I think I understand the tangle of ode classes now. I think it's much too complicated and that's why I was struggling with it. I'm sure we can simplify, if you want to go through with it.

Just to be clear, this change you're proposing has no affect on existing timing. It just allows you, an expert that's willing to hack the C++, to write analytic sensitivities and Jacobians, which, in this case, is a 2x speedup. (Or... does this speed up all of the odes in general? if so, I missed it and would like to know how / why.)

Daniel

On Thu, Aug 4, 2016 at 4:25 PM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi!
>
> I intend to refactor the current coupled ode system object. For one reason I would like to align ODE codes (rk45 and bdf) and for two I would like to route execution through the ode_system object. The reason to do so is that we can plug into the system analytic Jacobians of the ODE wrt to states and parameters using partial template specialization's.
>
> To illustrate what I mean, I prepared a "test" which has the sole purpose to show the execution time for the two cases (with AD and without AD):
>
> https://github.com/stan-dev/math/blob/feature/issue-310-coupled_ode_system-refactor-only/test/unit/math/rev/mat/functor/integrate_ode_rk45_noAD_test.cpp
>
> The speed gain for the specific case is close to 2x. This always depends on the ODE system, parameters, etc.. the speed gain will be larger for stiffer systems and for ODE systems with many states (this is my personal guess; the cases with many Jacobian evaluations). Applying this during model inference gave me 2-3x speedups.
>

Hi Sebastian,

Thanks for the comments and your code. For now I just want to comment on the following regarding the steady-state case.

> - steady-state conditions (although I have regular dosing); but I am not sure as to how this is > implemented in Torsten as it needs an implicit equation solver which we do not have yet in
> Stan - sundials has such a solver with sensitivity support

The way I have formulated the periodic steady-state case resulting from multiple dosing is in terms of:
y'(t) = f(t, y(t)),
where
y(t) = y(t + tau).
It is sufficient to collapse the latter condition to
y(0) = y(tau).
In other words it is a boundary value problem. In the past I handled that using a numerical root solver to solve for the initial conditions required to satisfy the last equation. Thus the initial value problem is embedded in the root solving problem.

You mention IDAS from the Sundials collection. It solves DAE systems of the form:
F(t, y(t), y'(t)) = 0
where
y(t0) = y0, y'(t0) = y'0.
I haven't figured out how to apply this to the aforementioned boundary value problem. I would be curious to know if you have formulated the steady-state problem in a way that IDAS could handle it. Otherwise I expected we would need to use some combination of the Stan ODE solvers with a root finder like KINSOL (also in Sundials).

Cheers,
Bill

On Friday, August 5, 2016 at 9:42:15 AM UTC-4, Daniel Lee wrote:
> If the goal is to have people write sensitivities and dense Jacobians in the Stan language, then what do you expect it to generate? Right now, we don't even allow users to specify gradients on their own functions and I think this is a good thing. Experts will be able to get into the C++ directly. I think it's hard to implement gradients correctly and not allowing users to try has saved us a lot of effort.

I would place zero weight on the problems of users who specify their own gradients incorrectly, but I think we need to provide mechanisms to do this (correctly). Now there are more and more packages that do like rstanarm and provide a set of pre-compiled models or do like brms and generate Stan code that could benefit from something like this. Hacking the C++ in those cases is not a good option because it would have to be done programatically.

Another thing that ties into this is the Stan requirement that user-defined functions be defined. If you declare a function in the functions block but don't define it, then the parser throws an error even though the pre-processor would be perfectly happy to find it in another .cpp file or the linker would be perfectly happy to find it in a shared object. If the parser would just delete that check, then it would be a lot easier to utilize custom C++ that might accumulate analytical gradients or whatever.

Ben

Hi Daniel,

My main goal is to have ODEs in Stan at maximum speed. I fully agree that AD is amazingly fast! However, in my field (any I guess many others as well) I need to solve essentially the same ODE in many projects such that it is very reasonable to work out Jacobians for those often used ODE systems. For the current stage I just would like to have an easy C++ way to make the analytic Jacobians possible for ODEs. It is in fact not so magic to do this - there are lots of tools out there to do automatic code generation already. So it comes down to knowing these tools and a bit of copy and paste. No magic. That does not mean this should be worked on in the future, i.e. having some Stan language features which help users with this, but we need to go in steps here.

The change I have put up does two things:

1. Use the ode_system for calculating the Jacobians. Doing so enables that specifying analytic Jacobians once will be beneficial for bdf and rk45 integrators in Stan

2. I made the coupled_ode_system work with an unshifted sensitivity system. Up to now the shifting was done whenever the initials vary. However, this is not needed at all and I aligned this with the CVODES code. This may lead to a minor speedup, not sure.

To be clear on this - yes there is no speed gain of the rk45 integrator by now using the ode_system (if at all only a very minor).

You appear to be very confused by the naming of ode_system - we did have a discussion on stab-dev about this (https://groups.google.com/forum/m/?fromgroups#!searchin/stan-dev/ode_system$20name/stan-dev/Bi4D_2YSrjI). Bob and Michael supported the name for it. The design of the ode_system object was aligned with Bob who suggested to use function name overloading. I myself like the ode_system name - it does reflect that this is the ODE plus needed facilities which is the Jacobian in this case.

Now, ode_system should really only provide the Jacobian and not the sensitivity system. The reason is that with the Jacobian it is straightforward to generate the sensitivity system which is needed (which depends on the case var/double and var/double for inits and parameters). Moreover, the CVODES code needs the Jacobian wrt to the states to do its stiff integration. I am not sure if renaming to dense_jacobian makes sense for a Stan object. I mean CVODES makes the distinction between sparse and dense jacobians while Stan always gives you a dense version of it as far as I am aware. So changing to dense_jacobian the function calls - I don’t know.

Moreover, the need to use the MatrixBase Eigen functionality is coming from the fact that I can then pass into the function Matrix and Map objects. The Map functionality enables to write directly into memory chunks, this is used here:

https://github.com/stan-dev/math/blob/develop/stan/math/rev/mat/functor/cvodes_ode_data.hpp#L105

or here:

https://github.com/stan-dev/math/blob/feature/issue-310-coupled_ode_system-refactor-only/stan/math/rev/mat/functor/coupled_ode_system.hpp#L439

If you require a Matrix to be passed around then this leads to extra copies which have to be created. From my experience this leads to a ~2-5% performance degradation.

So here is what I would suggest to do:

1. We move the coupled_ode_system to use the ode_system AND to not anymore do a shifting operation (which is on the branch for feature 310)

2. We make cvodes_ode_data use the couple_ode_system which would then be possible as no more shifting is done. Now, this will lead to a minor performance hit for the bdf integrator whenever users supply the analytic Jacobians. The reason is that then the coupled_ode_system cannot be instructed to calculate only the sensitivity system, but not evaluate the function itself. As this is not the major use case of coupled_ode_system and probably the performance hit is not too large, this would be ok. This would lead to a removal of all the rhs_sens function floating around in cvodes_ode_data.

However, we will still need the cvodes_ode_data object around as this is needed for the CVODES integrator for the static callback. The name of the object stems from the CVODES notion here which refers to this callback „thing“ as user data.

Best,
Sebastian

Right now, we don't even allow users to specify gradients on their own functions and I think this is a good thing. Experts will be able to get into the C++ directly. I think it's hard to implement gradients correctly and not allowing users to try has saved us a lot of effort.
>
> I think I understand the tangle of ode classes now. I think it's much too complicated and that's why I was struggling with it. I'm sure we can simplify, if you want to go through with it.
>
> Just to be clear, this change you're proposing has no affect on existing timing. It just allows you, an expert that's willing to hack the C++, to write analytic sensitivities and Jacobians, which, in this case, is a 2x speedup. (Or... does this speed up all of the odes in general? if so, I missed it and would like to know how / why.)
>
>
>
> Daniel
>
>
>
> On Thu, Aug 4, 2016 at 4:25 PM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi!
> >
> > I intend to refactor the current coupled ode system object. For one reason I would like to align ODE codes (rk45 and bdf) and for two I would like to route execution through the ode_system object. The reason to do so is that we can plug into the system analytic Jacobians of the ODE wrt to states and parameters using partial template specialization's.
> >
> > To illustrate what I mean, I prepared a "test" which has the sole purpose to show the execution time for the two cases (with AD and without AD):

> > https://github.com/stan-dev/math/blob/feature/issue-310-coupled_ode_system-refactor-only/test/unit/math/rev/mat/functor/integrate_ode_rk45_noAD_test.cpp
> >
> > The speed gain for the specific case is close to 2x. This always depends on the ODE system, parameters, etc.. the speed gain will be larger for stiffer systems and for ODE systems with many states (this is my personal guess; the cases with many Jacobian evaluations). Applying this during model inference gave me 2-3x speedups.
> >
> > Supplying the analytic Jacobians won't be something regular users will, rather only advanced users. Making this user friendly is a different topic (I can share some R codes which help already a lot).
> >
> > I hold on for the moment with a pull request until the design is settled.

>
> The way I have formulated the periodic steady-state case resulting from multiple dosing is in terms of:
> y'(t) = f(t, y(t)),
> where
> y(t) = y(t + tau).
> It is sufficient to collapse the latter condition to
> y(0) = y(tau).
> In other words it is a boundary value problem. In the past I handled that using a numerical root solver to solve for the initial conditions required to satisfy the last equation. Thus the initial value problem is embedded in the root solving problem.
>
> You mention IDAS from the Sundials collection. It solves DAE systems of the form:
> F(t, y(t), y'(t)) = 0
> where
> y(t0) = y0, y'(t0) = y'0.
> I haven't figured out how to apply this to the aforementioned boundary value problem. I would be curious to know if you have formulated the steady-state problem in a way that IDAS could handle it. Otherwise I expected we would need to use some combination of the Stan ODE solvers with a root finder like KINSOL (also in Sundials).

> Cheers,

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] refactor coupled_ode_system to use ode_system
messages.body_plain:
On Sat, Aug 6, 2016 at 3:25 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi Daniel,
>
> My main goal is to have ODEs in Stan at maximum speed. I fully agree that AD is amazingly fast! However, in my field (any I guess many others as well) I need to solve essentially the same ODE in many projects such that it is very reasonable to work out Jacobians for those often used ODE systems. For the current stage I just would like to have an easy C++ way to make the analytic Jacobians possible for ODEs. It is in fact not so magic to do this - there are lots of tools out there to do automatic code generation already. So it comes down to knowing these tools and a bit of copy and paste. No magic. That does not mean this should be worked on in the future, i.e. having some Stan language features which help users with this, but we need to go in steps here.
>
> The change I have put up does two things:
>
> 1. Use the ode_system for calculating the Jacobians. Doing so enables that specifying analytic Jacobians once will be beneficial for bdf and rk45 integrators in Stan
>
> 2. I made the coupled_ode_system work with an unshifted sensitivity system. Up to now the shifting was done whenever the initials vary. However, this is not needed at all and I aligned this with the CVODES code. This may lead to a minor speedup, not sure.
>
> To be clear on this - yes there is no speed gain of the rk45 integrator by now using the ode_system (if at all only a very minor).

And there's no speed gain for the BDF integrator also. Unless someone writes custom Jacobians. That's a good use case, this doesn't actually affect the existing code base in speed.

>
> You appear to be very confused by the naming of ode_system - we did have a discussion on stab-dev about this (https://groups.google.com/forum/m/?fromgroups#!searchin/stan-dev/ode_system$20name/stan-dev/Bi4D_2YSrjI). Bob and Michael supported the name for it. The design of the ode_system object was aligned with Bob who suggested to use function name overloading. I myself like the ode_system name - it does reflect that this is the ODE plus needed facilities which is the Jacobian in this case.

Here's the thread (the last link didn't go anywhere):
https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-dev/Bi4D_2YSrjI/ifd8mWKxBQAJ

I just looked at the thread again and I think it's a lot clearer now. I still don't like "ode_system" because I don't think "system" conveys the right information. I believe the original use of "coupled_ode_system" came from a the terminology used in odes, "system of equations" -- so the coupled ode system was not just the original ode system of equations, but now a new ode system of equations with the initial conditions and parameters coupled into the system.

I would think F is the ode_system and what you're describing is a way to wrap F and get sensitivities. So I'd just prefer a much more descriptive name that doesn't overload what we take to be the existing ode_system.

>
> Now, ode_system should really only provide the Jacobian and not the sensitivity system. The reason is that with the Jacobian it is straightforward to generate the sensitivity system which is needed (which depends on the case var/double and var/double for inits and parameters). Moreover, the CVODES code needs the Jacobian wrt to the states to do its stiff integration. I am not sure if renaming to dense_jacobian makes sense for a Stan object. I mean CVODES makes the distinction between sparse and dense jacobians while Stan always gives you a dense version of it as far as I am aware. So changing to dense_jacobian the function calls - I don’t know.

Then why do we have both?
In the integrator we have now, do we ever use both?
Do the "sparse Jacobians" and "dense Jacobians" line up with CVODES calls to rhs_sens() and dense_jacobian()? Or are they different?

(those are actual questions.... not sure what the answers are and if I'm missing something)

>
> Moreover, the need to use the MatrixBase Eigen functionality is coming from the fact that I can then pass into the function Matrix and Map objects. The Map functionality enables to write directly into memory chunks, this is used here:
>
> https://github.com/stan-dev/math/blob/develop/stan/math/rev/mat/functor/cvodes_ode_data.hpp#L105
>
> or here:
>
> https://github.com/stan-dev/math/blob/feature/issue-310-coupled_ode_system-refactor-only/stan/math/rev/mat/functor/coupled_ode_system.hpp#L439
>
> If you require a Matrix to be passed around then this leads to extra copies which have to be created. From my experience this leads to a ~2-5% performance degradation.

Ok. That makes sense. I stop doing Eigen Matrix stuff for a few weeks and I forgot how messy it looks.

> So here is what I would suggest to do:
>
> 1. We move the coupled_ode_system to use the ode_system AND to not anymore do a shifting operation (which is on the branch for feature 310)

I don't understand what this means. What is a "shifting operator"?

What part of the coupled_ode_system needs to use the ode_system?

Can we add a step 0 and rename ode_system? (Either that or give me a good name for the functor F, the system of ordinary differential equations.... if you tell me that's called something else in the literature, then I'll start referring to that as something else and we can leave this is "ode_system.")

>
> 2. We make cvodes_ode_data use the couple_ode_system which would then be possible as no more shifting is done. Now, this will lead to a minor performance hit for the bdf integrator whenever users supply the analytic Jacobians. The reason is that then the coupled_ode_system cannot be instructed to calculate only the sensitivity system, but not evaluate the function itself. As this is not the major use case of coupled_ode_system and probably the performance hit is not too large, this would be ok. This would lead to a removal of all the rhs_sens function floating around in cvodes_ode_data.
>
> However, we will still need the cvodes_ode_data object around as this is needed for the CVODES integrator for the static callback. The name of the object stems from the CVODES notion here which refers to this callback „thing“ as user data.

Sorry -- I couldn't follow along since I don't understand what shifting is.

Before you go forward, mind putting out a design first? I hate to say it, but UML or a flowchart might be helpful. I've had to use pen and paper multiple times to get a handle on how things get called. (I get it... you think it's all straightforward, but to me it isn't. I'm usually ok bouncing functionality between 2 classes... when it gets beyond that, it starts becoming a lot of effort.)

Alternatively, we could design the whole thing top-down leaving all the user-facing interfaces intact. We can write out the requirements (things we must have) and work from there.

Daniel

>
> Best,
> Sebastian
>

> > Am 05.08.2016 um 15:42 schrieb Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu>:
> >

> > Hi Sebastian,
> >
> > I think I see what's going on. Let me try to get everyone on board.
> >
> > These are the three relevant files to look at:
> > oral_2cmt.hpp <https://github.com/stan-dev/math/blob/feature/issue-310-coupled_ode_system-refactor-only/test/unit/math/rev/mat/functor/oral_2cmt.hpp>
> > The functor defined here is very close to what would be translated from Stan to C++.
> > ode_system.hpp <https://github.com/stan-dev/math/blob/300a769011fb7a53aeff495deee6e155280a5ee1/stan/math/rev/mat/functor/ode_system.hpp>
> > The first functor is passed into this class, ode_system, to calculate Jacobians. Jacobians are required by CVODES. ode_system takes the functor and uses automatic differentiation to compute Jacobians.
> > oral_2cmt_jacobian.hpp <https://github.com/stan-dev/math/blob/feature/issue-310-coupled_ode_system-refactor-only/test/unit/math/rev/mat/functor/oral_2cmt_jacobian.hpp>
> > This is a template specialization of the second file, ode_system, but for the oral_2cmt functor. Here, the Jacobians are known analytically so they're computed using doubles and without automatic differentiation.
> > This is a specialization for just that particular functor and is written in C++. This is currently not generated from the Stan language. In order to write analytic Jacobians in this way, a user needs to perform surgery on the generated code, but it can be done.
> > Some comments in no particular order:
> > I'm really pleased that autodiff is only 2x as long as putting in analytic gradients! That's awesome! I know this is a simpler example, but still... that's really rad.
> > I think there are changes we can make to ode_system to make things a lot better:
> > Rename. It's not an ode system. It's the Jacobians of an ode system. There are three functions exposed:
> > 1. A function to calculate the value of the ode at the time and state provided.
> > 2. A function to calculate the Jacobian of the RHS with respect to y.
> > 3. A function to calculate the Jacobians of the RHS with respect to y and the RHS with respect to theta.
> > Clean up the interface. I don't think it needs to be this complicated. For example, here are the three function signatures I would provide:
> > std::vector<double> operator()(double t, const std::vector<double>& y). returns dy_dt.
> > For the two Jacobian functions, I would simplify a lot and just use Eigen::Matrix<double, Dynamic, Dynamic> (or whatever the right type is). Having the indirection of Eigen::MatrixBase<Derived1> where Derived1 is a template parameter isn't helping. These things are double based containers and it would help a lot if it weren't overengineered. Unless there's a use-case that I'm missing. It doesn't look like there is, though.
> > I'd rethink cvodes_ode_data.hpp. I don't understand the naming. Now that I look at it, why aren't the functions in the existing ode_system.hpp renamed to rhs_sens() and dense_jacobian()? Would that be more descriptive?
> > What are your use cases for having people specify analytic Jacobians? (I guess CVODES is calling them sensitivities and dense Jacobians.)
> > If the goal is to have a user be able to hack the C++, I think it's sufficient to rename and clean up ode_system. And possibly cvodes_ode_data as well.
> > If the goal is to have people write sensitivities and dense Jacobians in the Stan language, then what do you expect it to generate? Right now, we don't even allow users to specify gradients on their own functions and I think this is a good thing. Experts will be able to get into the C++ directly. I think it's hard to implement gradients correctly and not allowing users to try has saved us a lot of effort.
> >
> > I think I understand the tangle of ode classes now. I think it's much too complicated and that's why I was struggling with it. I'm sure we can simplify, if you want to go through with it.
> >
> > Just to be clear, this change you're proposing has no affect on existing timing. It just allows you, an expert that's willing to hack the C++, to write analytic sensitivities and Jacobians, which, in this case, is a 2x speedup. messages.body_plain:
The only issue with users specifying wrong gradients is that
they'll get lots of divergences and either live with the wrong
answer or clog our mailing lists.  We do have checks that they've
defined it properly, but they're slow.

We could remove the requirement that functions are defined if
they are declared, but then there would be Stan programs that
translate to C++ but don't link.  I don't know how to catch the
error at that point and do something reasonable for the user.

I do want to support some kind of user-defined C++ extensions
for functions.

- Bob

> On Aug 5, 2016, at 11:46 AM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> On Friday, August 5, 2016 at 9:42:15 AM UTC-4, Daniel Lee wrote:
> 	• If the goal is to have people write sensitivities and dense Jacobians in the Stan language, then what do you expect it to generate? Right now, we don't even allow users to specify gradients on their own functions and I think this is a good thing. Experts will be able to get into the C++ directly. I think it's hard to implement gradients correctly and not allowing users to try has saved us a lot of effort.

> I would place zero weight on the problems of users who specify their own gradients incorrectly,

They'll get frustrated and blame us and clog our mailing list.
I don't want to make a policy of don't post X or Y.  So it's
going to cause work.  I could live with that, though.

> but I think we need to provide mechanisms to do this (correctly). Now there are more and more packages that do like rstanarm and provide a set of pre-compiled models or do like brms and generate Stan code that could benefit from something like this. Hacking the C++ in those cases is not a good option because it would have to be done programatically.
>
> Another thing that ties into this is the Stan requirement that user-defined functions be defined. If you declare a function in the functions block but don't define it, then the parser throws an error even though the pre-processor would be perfectly happy to find it in another .cpp file or the linker would be perfectly happy to find it in a shared object. If the parser would just delete that check, then it would be a lot easier to utilize custom C++ that might accumulate analytical gradients or whatever.

We could delete that check easily enough, but then what

>
> Ben

> Thanks for the comments and your code. For now I just want to comment on the following regarding the steady-state case.
>
>> - steady-state conditions (although I have regular dosing); but I am not sure as to how this is > implemented in Torsten as it needs an implicit equation solver which we do not have yet in
>> Stan - sundials has such a solver with sensitivity support
>
> The way I have formulated the periodic steady-state case resulting from multiple dosing is in terms of:
> y'(t) = f(t, y(t)),
> where
> y(t) = y(t + tau).
> It is sufficient to collapse the latter condition to
> y(0) = y(tau).
> In other words it is a boundary value problem. In the past I handled that using a numerical root solver to solve for the initial conditions required to satisfy the last equation. Thus the initial value problem is embedded in the root solving problem.
>
> You mention IDAS from the Sundials collection. It solves DAE systems of the form:
> F(t, y(t), y'(t)) = 0
> where
> y(t0) = y0, y'(t0) = y'0.
> I haven't figured out how to apply this to the aforementioned boundary value problem. I would be curious to know if you have formulated the steady-state problem in a way that IDAS could handle it. Otherwise I expected we would need to use some combination of the Stan ODE solvers with a root finder like KINSOL (also in Sundials).
>
> Cheers,
> Bill

messages.subject: parallelization - working prototype!!!
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

This is quite exciting... evaluating ODEs for many subjects is very costly and screams for threaded parallelization, i.e. to allocate multiple CPUs per chain and then execute the ODE integration per patient on multiple CPUs in parallel.

So far there were two problems and I have possibly found a solution to both of these:

1. threading... well, openmp just does the job. The nice thing is that any compiler not supporting openmp will just execute things serially (default clang on MacOS is such a case, but gcc 4.6 can run openmp)

2. the second big fat problem was to get autodiff to play with the threading... there is a very simple solution to this: Just don't use autodiff - that solves the problem!

Not using AD during ODE integration is possible as long as one supplies an ode_system object which calculates analytically the Jacobian.

Now, this approach should be usable for about any very expensive operation we have! I mean we anyway use pre-computed gradients for our expensive operations. ODEs is just one of those; I guess there is more.

So the solution to get multiple CPUs per chain may be darn simple - only parallelize stuff which does not use AD; of course, having AD things being parallel would even be better, but this is a start. Moreover, I am absolutely confident that applying this approach to ODEs will be a BIG step forward for Stan. I know, there are more problems to overcome, but this is a very straightforward possibility now.

Ahh, I forgot: I have a working prototype which grabs 2 CPUs and happily crunches the ODE system in 26s while on a single CPU it takes twice the time, 52s - this should give major speedups during inference.

Best,
Sebastian

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] parallelization - working prototype!!!
messages.body_plain:
That's fantastic.  It should give you pretty close to
an N times speedup with N cores if memory contention doesn't
become a bottleneck.  And you can run multiple groups of
cores on different physical machines for different chains.

We can do the same thing for matrix operations and
linear algebra because we're mainly doing the heavy
lifting with double values at this point.

I don't know how to roll parallelism into the language
for general use.  Any ideas?

For this case, it could tie into some specialized
functions that evaluate in parallel for parallel ODEs.

An alternative that would deal with autodiff would be
to do thread-specific nested autodiff.  There's a performance
hit to doing that of about 20% I think vs. running
single threaded.  Then as long as the entire function
(solving all the ODEs) can be tied up with gradients for
the outside, it should work.

Does OpenMP run cross platform?  If not, we'll have to figure
out some platform-specific runs.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] parallelization - working prototype!!!
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

To my knowledge OpenMP is cross-platform: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OpenMP

So this includes Windows! You only need a compiler which supports it. The clang++ on Macos does not support it at the moment, but you can install clang-omp as I understood. Moreover, compilers not supporting the OpenMP directives will simply just ignore it.

There is one caveat to take care of - exceptions must not propagate outside of an OpenMP thread. I remember that on stackoverflow there were some solutions suggested which take care of this (roughly speaking you catch all exceptions during parallelism and then rethrow as needed).

So a pfor construct would be great, but then we need to figure out how to detect code which can run in parallel. No idea how to do that (traits in C++?).

Another idea would be to have functions with a "_par" suffix for which users must specify the gradients. Then we allow only _par functions to be called in a pfor loop. For example.

For the ODE stuff... I know there is still some work to be done. I mean for PK problems I would have to stop and restart the integrator from time to time; no idea how to do this at this stage. I guess we would need to have the event handling inside Stan.

I also expect the speedup to scale really nicely with # of CPUs...just awesome. What Ben suggests to parallelize over the tree which gets build up sounds also very appealing.

I am really looking forward to throw a single chain onto one of our 20 CPU computing nodes.

Best,
Sebastian

Hi Daniel,

With the shifting operation I am referring to the process of setting initials to zero which is done in the coupled_ode_system whenever the initials vary. This is why this add_initals function was needed during decoupling of the ODE states. This shifting operation is not needed if you just setup the initial values of the sensitivity states a bit differently.

How about we call the functor F simply ode_rhs - with the understanding that this refers to the bare base system only. The ode_system is then the ode_rhs together with the Jacobians.

I have never used UML, so it would be very hard to me to layout the design using UML from scratch. Chances are better if I modify an existing UML for the current rk45 design. Does that exist? Is there a UML flowchart for any of the Stan sub-systems?

As a first step we could write on a wiki page definitions of things - or could we make the PDF I have written a while ago (under the link you quoted) sticky in the wiki?

For the current stage I just would like to have an easy C++ way to make the analytic Jacobians possible for ODEs. It is in fact not so magic to do this - there are lots of tools out there to do automatic code generation already. So it comes down to knowing these tools and a bit of copy and paste. No magic. Bob and Michael supported the name for it. The design of the ode_system object was aligned with Bob who suggested to use function name overloading. I myself like the ode_system name - it does reflect that this is the ODE plus needed facilities which is the Jacobian in this case.
>
>
> Here's the thread (the last link didn't go anywhere):
> https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-dev/Bi4D_2YSrjI/ifd8mWKxBQAJ
>
>
> I just looked at the thread again and I think it's a lot clearer now. I still don't like "ode_system" because I don't think "system" conveys the right information. I believe the original use of "coupled_ode_system" came from a the terminology used in odes, "system of equations" -- so the coupled ode system was not just the original ode system of equations, but now a new ode system of equations with the initial conditions and parameters coupled into the system.

> I would think F is the ode_system and what you're describing is a way to wrap F and get sensitivities. So I'd just prefer a much more descriptive name that doesn't overload what we take to be the existing ode_system.

>

The reason is that with the Jacobian it is straightforward to generate the sensitivity system which is needed (which depends on the case var/double and var/double for inits and parameters). Moreover, the CVODES code needs the Jacobian wrt to the states to do its stiff integration. I am not sure if renaming to dense_jacobian makes sense for a Stan object. So changing to dense_jacobian the function calls - I don’t know.

> std::vector<double> operator()(double t, const std::vector<double>& y). returns dy_dt.

I think it's hard to implement gradients correctly and not allowing users to try has saved us a lot of effort.

messages.body_plain:
On Sun, Aug 07, 2016 at 04:53:05PM -0700, Ben Goodrich wrote:
>    I am continuing to think that the next lowest hanging fruit (having
>    already parallelized chains) is to parallelize the leapfrog steps
>    rather than parellelizing within a leapfrog step.

That sounds like a good idea.

In OpenMx, we often use BFGS optimizers with a numerical approximation
of the gradient. An approach we took is to parallelize the numerical
approximation of the gradient. This works well because the central
difference algorithm requires 2 * #parameters evaluations of the fit
(usually more than the # of cores) and each evaluation is roughly the
same amount of work (so the work is evenly distributed among the cores).

--

I added a note to the function implementation page explaining
where to put function imlementation files:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Contributing-New-Functions-to-Stan

P.S.  Here's what I added:

Directories for code
--------------------

In general, implementations should go int the lowest directory possible, subject to the orderings

 scal < arr < mat

 prim < rev < mix;

 prim < fwd < mix;

If the left-hand type occurs, the directory has to be at least the minimum on the right

  Code includes     directory must be at least
  -------------     --------------------------
  Eigen::Matrix     mat
  std::vector       arr
  stan::math::rev   rev
  stan::math::fwd   fwd

Everything else follows from these two rules. The directories are laid out two deep, with

(prim | fwd | rev | mix) / (scal | arr | mat)

...

Depending on where you put the function (see the rules above), you'll need to include its definition file in the appropriate header include to make sure it's visible to models.  For instance, if the function is going into `stan/math/rev/arr/foo.hpp` then `#include <stan/math/rev/arr/foo.hpp>` should be included added to `stan/math/rev/arr.hpp`.

> On Aug 7, 2016, at 7:53 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

> On Sunday, August 7, 2016 at 1:52:14 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I don't know how to roll parallelism into the language
> for general use.  Any ideas?
>
> OpenMP --- for our purposes --- is basically just a way to parallelize for loops. So, I think we would either need to have the parser not strip out lines with # so that users could do OpenMP stuff themselves
>
> #pragma omp parallel for
> for (i in 1:N) {
>   // do safe stuff in parallel
> }
>
> which I suggested two and a half years ago
>
> https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/439
>
> or introduce a parallel for loop construct in the Stan language like
>
> pfor (i in 1:N) {
>   // do safe stuff in parallel
> }
>
> that parses to
>
> #pragma omp parallel for
> for (int = 1; i < N; i++) {
>   // do safe stuff in parallel
> }
>
> But I don't know how we would detect whether the body of the for loop is parallel safe or not.

Adding the pragma would be trivial, but it doesn't buy
us anything.

The problem is that neither of our two key operations are thread safe:

  * autodiff

  * incrementing log density

What we need to do is run
each of the pieces with what the autodiff folks call "pre-accumulation"
mode --- that is, calculate the partials of input with respect
to output in each parallel segment and then put everything together.

Almost everything we do can be broken down into adding into
the log density, so we could try synchronizing there.  Then
we'd need each of the autodiff pieces to run in their own sandbox
to produce something that could be synched into the log density.

I'm not sure parallel loops is the right abstraction here (as
opposed to say, a work queue of functions to evaluate, each
in its own autodiff sandbox to produce a pre-accumulated result
(output and partials to all inputs) that could then be synched
back into the result.

messages.body_plain:
Finite differencing is embarassingly parallel.

And you could do the same thing with forward mode autodiff to
compute gradients, but it's not worth it when you have
reverse mode autodiff---you'd need N CPUs where N is the
number of parameters for maybe a factor of 2 speedup.

Where parallelism would be hugely helpful would be in Jacobian
calculations for multivariate functions and in (dense or diagonal)
Hessians.

- Bob

target back through normal_lpdf back to the parameters in the

using purely double values.

> > On Aug 8, 2016, at 3:48 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi Daniel,
> >
> > With the shifting operation I am referring to the process of setting initials to zero which is done in the coupled_ode_system whenever the initials vary. This is why this add_initals function was needed during decoupling of the ODE states. This shifting operation is not needed if you just setup the initial values of the sensitivity states a bit differently.
> >
> > How about we call the functor F simply ode_rhs - with the understanding that this refers to the bare base system only. The ode_system is then the ode_rhs together with the Jacobians.
> >
> > I have never used UML, so it would be very hard to me to layout the design using UML from scratch. Chances are better if I modify an existing UML for the current rk45 design. Does that exist? Is there a UML flowchart for any of the Stan sub-systems?

> > On Saturday, August 6, 2016 at 3:43:39 PM UTC+2, Daniel Lee wrote:
> >> On Sat, Aug 6, 2016 at 3:25 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
> >>
> >>
> >> Hi Daniel,
> >>
> >>
> >> My main goal is to have ODEs in Stan at maximum speed. I fully agree that AD is amazingly fast! However, in my field (any I guess many others as well) I need to solve essentially the same ODE in many projects such that it is very reasonable to work out Jacobians for those often used ODE systems. For the current stage I just would like to have an easy C++ way to make the analytic Jacobians possible for ODEs. It is in fact not so magic to do this - there are lots of tools out there to do automatic code generation already. So it comes down to knowing these tools and a bit of copy and paste. No magic. That does not mean this should be worked on in the future, i.e. having some Stan language features which help users with this, but we need to go in steps here.
> >>
> >>
> >> The change I have put up does two things:
> >>
> >>
> >> 1. Use the ode_system for calculating the Jacobians. Doing so enables that specifying analytic Jacobians once will be beneficial for bdf and rk45 integrators in Stan
> >>
> >>
> >> 2. I made the coupled_ode_system work with an unshifted sensitivity system. Up to now the shifting was done whenever the initials vary. However, this is not needed at all and I aligned this with the CVODES code. This may lead to a minor speedup, not sure.
> >>
> >>
> >> To be clear on this - yes there is no speed gain of the rk45 integrator by now using the ode_system (if at all only a very minor).
> >>
> >>
> >> And there's no speed gain for the BDF integrator also. Unless someone writes custom Jacobians. That's a good use case, this doesn't actually affect the existing code base in speed.
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >> You appear to be very confused by the naming of ode_system - we did have a discussion on stab-dev about this (https://groups.google.com/forum/m/?fromgroups#!searchin/stan-dev/ode_system$20name/stan-dev/Bi4D_2YSrjI). Bob and Michael supported the name for it. The design of the ode_system object was aligned with Bob who suggested to use function name overloading. I myself like the ode_system name - it does reflect that this is the ODE plus needed facilities which is the Jacobian in this case.
> >>
> >>
> >> Here's the thread (the last link didn't go anywhere):
> >> https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-dev/Bi4D_2YSrjI/ifd8mWKxBQAJ
> >>
> >>
> >> I just looked at the thread again and I think it's a lot clearer now. I still don't like "ode_system" because I don't think "system" conveys the right information. I believe the original use of "coupled_ode_system" came from a the terminology used in odes, "system of equations" -- so the coupled ode system was not just the original ode system of equations, but now a new ode system of equations with the initial conditions and parameters coupled into the system.
> >>
> >>
> >> I would think F is the ode_system and what you're describing is a way to wrap F and get sensitivities. So I'd just prefer a much more descriptive name that doesn't overload what we take to be the existing ode_system.
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >> Now, ode_system should really only provide the Jacobian and not the sensitivity system. The reason is that with the Jacobian it is straightforward to generate the sensitivity system which is needed (which depends on the case var/double and var/double for inits and parameters). Moreover, the CVODES code needs the Jacobian wrt to the states to do its stiff integration. I am not sure if renaming to dense_jacobian makes sense for a Stan object. I mean CVODES makes the distinction between sparse and dense jacobians while Stan always gives you a dense version of it as far as I am aware. So changing to dense_jacobian the function calls - I don’t know.
> >>
> >>
> >> Then why do we have both?
> >> In the integrator we have now, do we ever use both?
> >> Do the "sparse Jacobians" and "dense Jacobians" line up with CVODES calls to rhs_sens() and dense_jacobian()? Or are they different?
> >>
> >>
> >> (those are actual questions.... not sure what the answers are and if I'm missing something)
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >> Moreover, the need to use the MatrixBase Eigen functionality is coming from the fact that I can then pass into the function Matrix and Map objects. The Map functionality enables to write directly into memory chunks, this is used here:
> >>
> >>
> >> https://github.com/stan-dev/math/blob/develop/stan/math/rev/mat/functor/cvodes_ode_data.hpp#L105
> >>
> >>
> >> or here:
> >>
> >>
> >> https://github.com/stan-dev/math/blob/feature/issue-310-coupled_ode_system-refactor-only/stan/math/rev/mat/functor/coupled_ode_system.hpp#L439
> >>
> >>
> >> If you require a Matrix to be passed around then this leads to extra copies which have to be created. From my experience this leads to a ~2-5% performance degradation.
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >> Ok. That makes sense. I stop doing Eigen Matrix stuff for a few weeks and I forgot how messy it looks.
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >> So here is what I would suggest to do:
> >>
> >>
> >> 1. We move the coupled_ode_system to use the ode_system AND to not anymore do a shifting operation (which is on the branch for feature 310)
> >>
> >>
> >> I don't understand what this means. What is a "shifting operator"?
> >>
> >>
> >> What part of the coupled_ode_system needs to use the ode_system?
> >>
> >>
> >> Can we add a step 0 and rename ode_system? (Either that or give me a good name for the functor F, the system of ordinary differential equations.... if you tell me that's called something else in the literature, then I'll start referring to that as something else and we can leave this is "ode_system.")
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >> 2. We make cvodes_ode_data use the couple_ode_system which would then be possible as no more shifting is done. Now, this will lead to a minor performance hit for the bdf integrator whenever users supply the analytic Jacobians. The reason is that then the coupled_ode_system cannot be instructed to calculate only the sensitivity system, but not evaluate the function itself. As this is not the major use case of coupled_ode_system and probably the performance hit is not too large, this would be ok. This would lead to a removal of all the rhs_sens function floating around in cvodes_ode_data.
> >>
> >>
> >> However, we will still need the cvodes_ode_data object around as this is needed for the CVODES integrator for the static callback. The name of the object stems from the CVODES notion here which refers to this callback „thing“ as user data.
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >> Sorry -- I couldn't follow along since I don't understand what shifting is.
> >>
> >>
> >> Before you go forward, mind putting out a design first? I hate to say it, but UML or a flowchart might be helpful. I've had to use pen and paper multiple times to get a handle on how things get called. (I get it... you think it's all straightforward, but to me it isn't. I'm usually ok bouncing functionality between 2 classes... when it gets beyond that, it starts becoming a lot of effort.)
> >>
> >>
> >> Alternatively, we could design the whole thing top-down leaving all the user-facing interfaces intact. We can write out the requirements (things we must have) and work from there.
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >> Daniel
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >> Best,
> >> Sebastian
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >> Am 05.08.2016 um 15:42 schrieb Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu>:
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >> Hi Sebastian,
> >>
> >>
> >> I think I see what's going on. Let me try to get everyone on board.
> >>
> >>
> >> These are the three relevant files to look at:
> >> oral_2cmt.hpp
> >> The functor defined here is very close to what would be translated from Stan to C++.
> >> ode_system.hpp
> >> The first functor is passed into this class, ode_system, to calculate Jacobians. Jacobians are required by CVODES. ode_system takes the functor and uses automatic differentiation to compute Jacobians. oral_2cmt_jacobian.hpp
> >> This is a template specialization of the second file, ode_system, but for the oral_2cmt functor. Here, the Jacobians are known analytically so they're computed using doubles and without automatic differentiation.
> >> This is a specialization for just that particular functor and is written in C++. This is currently not generated from the Stan language. In order to write analytic Jacobians in this way, a user needs to perform surgery on the generated code, but it can be done.
> >> Some comments in no particular order:
> >> I'm really pleased that autodiff is only 2x as long as putting in analytic gradients! That's awesome! I know this is a simpler example, but still... that's really rad.I think there are changes we can make to ode_system to make things a lot better:Rename. It's not an ode system. It's the Jacobians of an ode system. There are three functions exposed:
> >> 1. A function to calculate the value of the ode at the time and state provided.
> >> 2. A function to calculate the Jacobian of the RHS with respect to y.
> >> 3. A function to calculate the Jacobians of the RHS with respect to y and the RHS with respect to theta.Clean up the interface. I don't think it needs to be this complicated. For example, here are the three function signatures I would provide:
> >> std::vector<double> operator()(double t, const std::vector<double>& y). returns dy_dt.
> >> For the two Jacobian functions, I would simplify a lot and just use Eigen::Matrix<double, Dynamic, Dynamic> (or whatever the right type is). Having the indirection of Eigen::MatrixBase<Derived1> where Derived1 is a template parameter isn't helping. These things are double based containers and it would help a lot if it weren't overengineered. Unless there's a use-case that I'm missing. It doesn't look like there is, though.
> >> I'd rethink cvodes_ode_data.hpp. I don't understand the naming. Now that I look at it, why aren't the functions in the existing ode_system.hpp renamed to rhs_sens() and dense_jacobian()? Would that be more descriptive?What are your use cases for having people specify analytic Jacobians? (I guess CVODES is calling them sensitivities and dense Jacobians.)If the goal is to have a user be able to hack the C++, I think it's sufficient to rename and clean up ode_system. And possibly cvodes_ode_data as well.If the goal is to have people write sensitivities and dense Jacobians in the Stan language, then what do you expect it to generate? Right now, we don't even allow users to specify gradients on their own functions and I think this is a good thing. Experts will be able to get into the C++ directly. I think it's hard to implement gradients correctly and not allowing users to try has saved us a lot of effort.
> >>
> >>
> >> I think I understand the tangle of ode classes now. I think it's much too complicated and that's why I was struggling with it. I'm sure we can simplify, if you want to go through with it.
> >>
> >>
> >> Just to be clear, this change you're proposing has no affect on existing timing. It just allows you, an expert that's willing to hack the C++, to write analytic sensitivities and Jacobians, which, in this case, is a 2x speedup. (Or... does this speed up all of the odes in general? if so, I missed it and would like to know how / why.)
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >> Daniel
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >> On Thu, Aug 4, 2016 at 4:25 PM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
> >> Hi!
> >>
> >> I intend to refactor the current coupled ode system object. For one reason I would like to align ODE codes (rk45 and bdf) and for two I would like to route execution through the ode_system object. The reason to do so is that we can plug into the system analytic Jacobians of the ODE wrt to states and parameters using partial template specialization's.
> >>
> >> To illustrate what I mean, I prepared a "test" which has the sole purpose to show the execution time for the two cases (with AD and without AD):
> >>
> >> https://github.com/stan-dev/math/blob/feature/issue-310-coupled_ode_system-refactor-only/test/unit/math/rev/mat/functor/integrate_ode_rk45_noAD_test.cpp
> >>
> >> The speed gain for the specific case is close to 2x. This always depends on the ODE system, parameters, etc.. the speed gain will be larger for stiffer systems and for ODE systems with many states (this is my personal guess; the cases with many Jacobian evaluations). Applying this during model inference gave me 2-3x speedups.
> >>
> >> Supplying the analytic Jacobians won't be something regular users will, rather only advanced users. Making this user friendly is a different topic (I can share some R codes which help already a lot).
> >>
> >> I hold on for the moment with a pull request until the design is settled.
> >>
> >> Best,
> >> Sebastian

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] parallelization - working prototype!!!
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

With OpenMP one can easily instruct the code to execute certain critical parts of the code only serially. Maybe this is the key to parallelize code which runs mainly with doubles and only very rarely needs access to the shared AD stack. The code parts which access the shared AD stack can be marked in order to perform the access in a serial order only. One can even request that the order of those code blocks must be done in order of execution of the wrapping for-loop.

Enforcing such ordering, which is internally handled with mutex locking and unlocking, will degrade the performance somewhat, but maybe it is a good compromise.

Sebastian

On Monday, August 8, 2016 at 10:04:35 PM UTC+2, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > On Aug 8, 2016, at 3:04 PM, Ben Goodrich
> >

> > On Monday, August 8, 2016 at 2:03:55 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > #pragma omp parallel for
> > > for (int = 1; i < N; i++) {
> > >   // do safe stuff in parallel
> > > }
> > >
> > > But I don't know how we would detect whether the body of the for loop is parallel safe or not.
> >
> > Adding the pragma would be trivial, but it doesn't buy
> > us anything.
> >
> > But that is pretty much all Sebastian was doing
> >
> > #pragma  omp parallel for
> > for (int i = 1; i < N; i++) {
> >   mu[i] = integrate_ode(...);
> > } // end parallel part
> > target += normal_lpdf(y | mu, sigma);
>
> If there aren't any parameters in the ..., then that's OK, because
> setting mu[i] for different i should be thread safe.
>
> The tricky part is getting the derivatives from mu[i] back down
> to the parameters for the ... bits.  I
>
>
> >
> > If the parallel loop only does assignment
>
> The key is the mu[i] assignment, which is disjoint across
> the loop iterations.  But you couldn't do sum += ... that way.
>
> > and doesn't involve any i - 1 stuff, then it is fine, right? The target += line is evaluated in the main thread.
>
> Right, but it needs the derivatives to be reconstructed from
> target back through normal_lpdf back to the parameters in the
> ... parts.  Sebastian's pulling out the parallel part to implement
> using purely double values.
>
> - Bob

> >
>
> > Thanks for the comments and your code. For now I just want to comment on the following regarding the steady-state case.

> >
>
> >> - steady-state conditions (although I have regular dosing); but I am not sure as to how this is > implemented in Torsten as it needs an implicit equation solver which we do not have yet in
>
> >> Stan - sundials has such a solver with sensitivity support
>
> >
>
> > The way I have formulated the periodic steady-state case resulting from multiple dosing is in terms of:
>
> > y'(t) = f(t, y(t)),
>
> > where
>
> > y(t) = y(t + tau).
>
> > It is sufficient to collapse the latter condition to
>
> > y(0) = y(tau).
>
> > In other words it is a boundary value problem. In the past I handled that using a numerical root solver to solve for the initial conditions required to satisfy the last equation. Thus the initial value problem is embedded in the root solving problem.
>
> >
>
> > You mention IDAS from the Sundials collection. It solves DAE systems of the form:
>
> > F(t, y(t), y'(t)) = 0
>
> > where
>
> > y(t0) = y0, y'(t0) = y'0.
>
> > I haven't figured out how to apply this to the aforementioned boundary value problem. I would be curious to know if you have formulated the steady-state problem in a way that IDAS could handle it. Otherwise I expected we would need to use some combination of the Stan ODE solvers with a root finder like KINSOL (also in Sundials).

> >
>
> > Cheers,

> >>> I read through (much of) your code and examples and I'm trying to understand the difference between the standard Stan ODE solver and your compartmental model functions.  I had a few thoughts:

> >>>
>
> >>> - Seems like PKModelTwoCpt (and the OneCpt version) are convenience functions in the sense that they wrap up those specific ODE systems for easy use.  They are not really pharma-specific in the sense that other modeling could use them (e.g.-geochemical systems).  Someday it might be nice to have a library of pre-implemented ODE's for a variety of model types like this and starting with pharma-related examples might be a nice thing but for Stan itself it might make more sense to cast them more broadly

Yes, but as I commented in my post on 8/5 I am not sure the periodic steady-state problem commonly encountered in PK can be handled by the usual DAE solvers, e.g., IDA from SUNDIALS.

Bill

> >
> >> - steady-state conditions (although I have regular dosing); but I am not sure as to how this is > implemented in Torsten as it needs an implicit equation solver which we do not have yet in
> >> Stan - sundials has such a solver with sensitivity support
> >
> > The way I have formulated the periodic steady-state case resulting from multiple dosing is in terms of:
> > y'(t) = f(t, y(t)),
> > where
> > y(t) = y(t + tau).
> > It is sufficient to collapse the latter condition to
> > y(0) = y(tau).
> > In other words it is a boundary value problem. In the past I handled that using a numerical root solver to solve for the initial conditions required to satisfy the last equation. Thus the initial value problem is embedded in the root solving problem.
> >
> > You mention IDAS from the Sundials collection. It solves DAE systems of the form:
> > F(t, y(t), y'(t)) = 0
> > where
> > y(t0) = y0, y'(t0) = y'0.
> > I haven't figured out how to apply this to the aforementioned boundary value problem. I would be curious to know if you have formulated the steady-state problem in a way that IDAS could handle it. Otherwise I expected we would need to use some combination of the Stan ODE solvers with a root finder like KINSOL (also in Sundials).
